extracted.intended_audience: practitioners (patent attorneys/agents) appearing before the USPTO; USPTO disciplinary and ethics stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules for professional conduct by practitioners before the USPTO, focused on competence, communication, handling of client funds and files, candor, dishonesty, and related sanctions considerations in patent practice and disciplinary investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must 'provide competent representation' requiring the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of incompetence include giving clients inaccurate information about the status of patent matters (e.g., falsely advising that applications were filed), allowing or signing inventor declarations not personally executed by the inventor, miscalculating or misstating filing dates and priority claims, and giving materially inaccurate legal advice (e.g., incorrectly stating USPTO procedures regarding recording trademark licenses or inventorship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abide by client's decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.102)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall abide by a client's decisions concerning the objectives of representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A violation occurs when the practitioner fails to follow client instructions regarding course of action — e.g., failing to file a patent application the client hired the practitioner to file, not filing a promised continuation-in-part (CIP), or filing for the wrong trademark verbiage despite client instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must 'act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to prepare, file, and prosecute patent applications in a timely manner (e.g., missing or risking the client's one-year grace period after public disclosure; repeatedly assuring imminent filings that are not made) constitutes lack of diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communication / keeping client informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must '[k]eep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter' and explain matters 'to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important communications (e.g., Office Actions, Notices of Publication) must be forwarded to the client; failing to notify the client of such documents or fabricating evidence of notification violates these duties. The rule also requires clear explanation of consequences (e.g., abandoned applications, international filing rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate basis or rate of fees (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must communicate to clients the basis or rate of the fees and expenses for which the client will be responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrepant or multiple 'final invoices' showing different balances without explanation, and failing to clarify or explain billing discrepancies to the client, violate this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling advance payments and client funds; no commingling (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(a) & (c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must deposit advance fees and expenses into a client trust account to be withdrawn only as earned or incurred and must hold clients' property separate from the practitioner's own property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing client advance payments into accounts holding the practitioner's own funds (commingling) or failing to deposit advances into trust constitutes serious ethical violations ('the cardinal sin' of the profession).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect client's interests on termination (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination, practitioner must 'take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client's interests,' including surrendering papers and property to which the client is entitled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to forward complete client files after termination, promising to transition files but not doing so, or producing fabricated documents purporting to show file transfer are violations of this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor to a tribunal / no false statements (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner 'shall not knowingly ... make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to the tribunal.' The USPTO is considered a tribunal for this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations include signing or allowing another to sign an inventor's declaration and filing it with the Office. A finding under this provision requires proof of knowing falsehood; the Tribunal will compare facts and precedents to determine whether conduct was knowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of such misconduct include repeatedly misrepresenting the filing status of patent matters to clients and successor counsel, fabricating an 'Acknowledgement Receipt' or other documents to mislead clients about performance of work, and fabricating client correspondence (emails/memos) to conceal failures. Intent to deceive is a key element for sanction under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice — behavior that negatively impacts the public's perception of the courts or legal profession or undermines public confidence in the legal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a patent application containing an inventor's declaration signed by someone other than the inventor and similar misconduct that undermines trust in the system can constitute a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor oath/declaration signature requirements (37 C.F.R. § 1.63; MPEP § 602.08(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: All patent applications must be accompanied by an oath or declaration personally executed by the inventor; electronically filed applications must contain an oath or declaration 'personally signed by the inventor' and 'only inventors can execute' the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uploading a declaration that was not personally signed by the named inventor (e.g., a signature typed or entered by someone else) can violate USPTO rules and constitute ethical misconduct under competence, candor, or dishonesty provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with disciplinary investigation requests / organization of exhibits (37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: When responding to Requests for Information and Evidence (RFIs) during investigations, practitioners must provide responsive information and exhibits in a clear, organized, and timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting disorganized collections (nested ZIP folders, duplicate files, empty folders, mislabeled items) that impede the investigator's ability to connect exhibits to responses undermines cooperation and can be cited against the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions determination factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) and ABA Standards guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining sanctions, the Tribunal must consider (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) the existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal often looks to the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance on appropriate length/severity of sanction and on aggravating/mitigating circumstances. Examples: dishonesty and commingling are aggravating; lack of intent may mitigate certain findings.
